# Brood Benchmarks — the qualitative read

**Live numbers live in [`results/report.md`](results/report.md)** (regenerated by the harness) and
the [positioning chart](results/positioning.svg). This file is the *interpretation*: where Brood
wins, where it loses, and why — without re-listing every number (which only goes stale).

Machine: `whklat`, 12-core x86-64, Linux 7.0.0 · Brood 0.1.0 · Elixir 1.20.0 / OTP 28 · Python
3.14.4 · Node 22.21.0 · Ruby 3.3.8 · .NET 10.0.109. Best of 5 runs (startup best of 15; the
concurrency rows best of 7). **compute = wall − startup**, so boot cost isn't charged against
compute-heavy work. Each run is `taskset`-pinned with a 0.25 s settle; every program prints one
integer and the harness asserts all six agree, so the work is provably equivalent.

## Where Brood stands

- **Memory** — ~24 MB base RSS, among the lightest of six (~tied with Ruby, well below Node, .NET,
  Elixir); only Python is lighter. Stays light even under `pfib`'s 12-core fan-out.
- **Startup** — ~37 ms, ahead of Ruby and ~5× ahead of the BEAM's ~200 ms boot.
- **Outright wins** — `strings` (**fastest of six**: the streaming `%string-join` kernel builds the
  result in one immutable pass) and concurrent I/O `http` (**2nd, behind only Node**).
- **Single-threaded compute** — **~8× off the fastest** (.NET) by the aggregate metric: 4th of six,
  ahead of Ruby (~10×) and well ahead of Python (~23×), behind the JITs (.NET, Node) and the BEAM.
  Beats both interpreters on most folds and recursion.

## What runs native vs interpreted

The tier-1 JIT covers integer self-tail loops (`loop`, `collatz`), float comparison loops
(`mandelbrot`), indexed array reads (`matmul`'s inner `dot`, via loop-invariant hoisting — sound
with no alias analysis because Brood data is immutable), and **non-tail recursion** (`fib`): a JIT'd
caller now links straight to a JIT'd callee through an **epoch-guarded, in-IR call-site fast-link**,
which took `fib` compute from ~502 → ~274 ms (~11× → ~7× off the fastest). A `def` deopts affected
code, so Emacs-style hot reload holds. Workers in `spawn`/`pfib` share one compiled copy of the
native code instead of each recompiling.

Still interpreted (the weak rows) — these bail the JIT and run the bytecode dispatch loop, which
profiling puts at ~60 % of an interpreted benchmark's time:

- **`nqueens` (~41×), `bintree` (~34×)** — backtracking + short-lived allocation the JIT doesn't
  cover; the per-step list/tree building dominates.
- **`errors-deep` (~34×)** — but this is the row where **.NET is *last*** (a full stack-trace
  capture per throw scales with depth); Brood is mid-pack, ahead of .NET. A compute-loop-only suite
  hides this real-world axis.
- **`wordcount` (~26×)** — *not* an immutability cost: Elixir's immutable `Map.update` is also far
  faster, so the gap is Brood's young CHAMP map's constant factors (two trie walks per update, no
  `map-update` primitive yet), not the persistent approach.
- **`matmul` (~8×)** — the inner loop is native; the residual is the one read LICM can't hoist (the
  per-`k` row) plus the boxed 24-byte `Value` vs .NET's register `long`.

`sort` (~3.5×) and `primes` (~5×) are Brood's closest compute gaps. `reduce` beats Node and Ruby
(Brood's primitive-reducer fast path undercuts their per-element callbacks). `pipeline` fuses via
lazy seq-views (`eduction` — one pass, no intermediate lists), matching the streaming forms its
peers use (Elixir `Stream`, Python generators, .NET LINQ).

## Concurrency

Brood uses green processes + message passing (the BEAM-style model). `http` is **2nd of six**
(behind Node), `pfib` and `spawn` finish ahead of Ruby and Python; the bare-metal runtimes (.NET,
Node) and the BEAM lead. These rows are load-sensitive — contention can shift the ratios.

## The frontier

None of the gaps are architectural — they're implementation headroom in a young runtime. The levers
are interpreter-dispatch cost and widening JIT coverage (allocation/recursion shapes, the immutable
map build). Brood is built for long-running apps (editors, web servers), so it spends some memory
for speed via the **mimalloc** backend. See [`results/report.md`](results/report.md) for the current
per-benchmark numbers and [`results/positioning.svg`](results/positioning.svg) for the compute-vs-memory map.
